title: Battle of Hong Kong
description:
Canada entered World War II in 1939, but the Canadian Army didn't participate in much combat for the first two years. The Prime Minister William Lyon Mackenzie King was careful about sending Canadian troops overseas, as he instead focused on military weapon production, food production, and the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan. In 1941, Britain requested Canadian troops to reinforce Hong Kong, even know they believed it was impossible to defend. Mackenzie King agreed, as he thought it wouldn't be very risky.

The Canadian troops that were sent to Hong Kong were composed of roughly 1,975 soilders from the Winnipeg Grenadiers and the Royal Rifles of Canada, arriving on November 16th, 1941. Neither regiment was really trained or prepared for a lot of combat, and a ton of soilders underestimated the Japanese military due to racism. On December 7th, 1941, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, and after another six hours they invaded Hong Kong.

The Japanese forces attacked the airfields and overwhelmed mainland defenses, which fell quickly. By December 13th, 1941, they lost the mainland, and the Allied troops retreated back to Hong Kong Island. They had no reinforcements, and they prepared for a final fight. They fought on the island for roughly two weeks under harsh conditions, eventually being left exhausted and outmatched.

The Battle of Hong kong lasted from December 8th to 25th, 1941, and ended with a surrender on Christmas. Throughout the battle, 290 Canadians were killed and 493 were wounded, and then another 264 died later in Japanese POW camps. After their surrender, the Canadian POWs were beaten, starved, and had to do forced labour, as the Japanese saw surrender as cowardly, making them treat Canadians with extreme cruelty and violence.

In August 1945, Japan eventually surrendered after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and food and medical aid were given to prisoner camps. The Battle of Hong Kong remains as one of the most signficant events in Canadian history, being the first land battle involving Canadian troops in World War II, and displaying the sacrifice of Canadians fighting under brutal conditions.

title: Dieppe Raid
description:
After the miracle of Dunkirk, the Allied forces were forced to retreat whilst Germany was pushing into Russian territory. The Allies weren't strong enough to pull off Operation Overlord, so instead they planned a smaller attack known as the Dieppe Raid. Their goal was to gain combat experience and test the strength of Allied equipment by targeting a port in France, with Canadian troops leading the main attack.

On May 20th, 1942, troops were positioned on the Isle of Wight, located in the English Channel, training for the operation. Due to poor weather conditions, the attack was delayed until August. The invading force was mainly made up of Canadians, with around 5000/6100 of the soilders being Canadian. The raid took place on the morning of August 19th, 1942, with the Allied forces attacking at five different points along the battlefront.

The attack was unsuccessful as the allies lost the element of suprise. The sharp and violent noises alerted the German defenses on the coast, allowing them to prepare and man their positions before the Allies arrived. As a result, the attack troops faced heavy fire almost immediately after they landed.

After nine hours of fighting, 907 Canadian soilders were killed, 2406 were wounded, and 1946 were taken prisoner. There were more Canadians captured during the Dieppe Raid than in eleven months of fighting in Northwest Europe between 1944 and 1945. The scale of the losses suprised allied leaders, as no one could have immagined how terrible the operation would turn out. The Dieppe Raid became one of the most significant defeats in Canadian military history.

title: Battle of the Atlantic
description:
The Battle of the Atlantic lasted from September 3rd, 1939, to May 8th, 1945, making it the longest continuous battle of World War II. Their goal was for the Allies to have control of the shipping lanes between North America and Europe in order to transport food, troops, and war supplies to Britain. This battle was really important to Canada, as Canada was responsible for shipping a lot of these supplies across the Atlantic. The first attack was on September 3rd, 1939, when the German U-boat U-30 sank the passenger ship SS Athenia, killing 112 people including four Canadians.

Canada's responsibility was to escort merchant ships sailing from Halifax, Sydney, and St. Johns. The first convoy, HX-1 left on September 16th, 1939, and was escorted by two Canadian destroyers, HMCS St. Laurent and HMCS Saguenay. At the beginning of the war, Canada's navy was very small, as there were only six destroyers and 3,500 sailors. Canada grew its navy by building many ships including smaller corvettes designed to protect convoys.

One of the most dangerous areas during the battle was the Black Pit located in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. This place was so dangerous as it was located far out of range for any Allied aircraft to reach, and thus was the site of many deadly attacks.In 1942, German U-boats reached Canadian and American coastlines, entering the Gulf of St. Lawrence and sinking 21 ships. This was the first time the combat had ever reached Canadian waters. At this time, Germany was at the peak of their success in the battle, roughly sinking a hundred ships per month. At the end of 1942, around 2,000 ships had been lost.

In 1943, the Allies started to make a comeback in the Battle of the Atlantic. They had crackled the Enigma code, developed aircraft that could fly much further, and made improved escort ships that protected convoys through the Black Pit. Allied losses dropped dramatically, with only 300 ships being lost in 1943 and the spring of 1944. Canadian ships sank 8 German U-boats between the end of 1943 and spring of 1944. The battle was still dangerous, as newer German U-boats developed advanced torpedoes able to lock onto propeller sounds. In September, 1943, the HMCS St. Croix was sunk by an acoustic torpedo, and almost all survivors were killed when the rescue ship was sunk as well.

By the final year of the war, eight Canadian warships had been sunk and four damaged, but Canada's navy had greatly increased in size. As the war was coming to an end, the Allies placed all naval forces stretching from Nova Scotia to the Arctic under Canadian command. By 1945, Canada possessed 487 warships, 90,000 sailors, 3,000 landing craft, and 400 cargo ships. The Battle of the Atlantic was vital for the Allied victory, as they needed to maintain the supply routes to Britain to win the war.

title: Battle of Vimy Ridge
description:
The Battle of Vimy Ridge occurred during World War I from April 9 to April 12, 1917. Canadian forces were fighting German troops over Vimy Ridge, a long and elevated mountain in France that was very well defended and nearly impossible to take over. The French military already knew about the ridge and lost 100,000 troops trying to take over the ridge, so there was no doubt about the ridge being almost unconquerable. A German hold for a long time, the ridge was fortified with trenches, barbed wire, and even tunnels.

Subsequent to the battle at Somme in the year 1916, an estimated 100,000 Canadian forces deployed in the region in preparation for battle. Instead of charging into battle unpreparedly, they took time to plan. They worked on repairing trenches and roads, laying down communication cables to the tune of over 100 kilometers. They constructed water and supply systems. Additionally, they excavated eleven tunnels beneath the battlefields in order to enable the safe movement of their troops towards the battlefront without coming into contact with gunfire from the enemy. The tunnels contained appropriate facilities such as light, water, and medical facilities.

The Canadians also adopted other techniques which proved to be of significant benefit to them. Maps and three-dimensional models of the ridge had been studied so that soldiers understood where they had to go even before the attack began. The objective of the infantry and artillery had been integrated, with each soldier assigned tasks such as machine gun and grenade positions. The Canadian artillery had lobbed over one million shells in just a week-long bombardment, which had ruined many of the German defenses. The Germans subsequently named this assault the “Week of Suffering” as it proved to be so intense.

The resulting biggest attack began at 5:30 A.M. on April 9, 1917, with the involvement of around 15,000 Canadian soldiers from the first wave of the attack. This ended with the successful capture of the Vimy Ridge after just four days of fierce battles and with the loss of 3,598 Canadian soldiers and around 7,000 more wounds. This successful engagement marked an essential step in the process of Canada obtaining the status of an independent state from the status of the British colony, as the Canadians successfully fought together altogether for the first time and proved their capabilities to the world.

title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
description:
The fall of the Berlin Wall occurred just five days after the massive procession of 500,000 people in East Berlin. It is remembered that on this particular night, thousands of people gathered by the wall, stood on top of it, and began pulling it down with whatever they had in their hands. Everyone had tears of joy in their eyes as they hugged each other, as for the past almost three decades, the wall had split not just families and friends but the entire nation apart.

Following the end of World War II, Germany was left divided between the Soviet Union, on one hand, and the other alliances on the other hand, located on the west side. Despite the fact that Berlin, a city within East Germany, Germany itself had been divided into four parts, namely one part for the Soviet Union, as well as another part for Britain, France, as well as the United States of America. The year 1961 witnessed the building of Berlin Walls by the government of East Germany, approved by the Soviet Union, dissuading individuals from relocating to West Berlin, as a result of the freedoms that existed alongside the democratic forms of rule.

The 1980s were a bad time for the Soviet Union and other communist states, as things were literally going to pieces there. Their economies were not strong, and people were suffering from shortages, as they were dissatisfied with their governments as well. The 1986 nuclear disaster in Ukraine’s Chernobyl plant made the entire situation look worse, as things were not being managed correctly there either. The people of Eastern Europe, as well as the East Germans, began protesting for a change.

The fall of the Berlin Wall, when it finally opened and began to come down, was more than just the tearing down of a wall. This symbolized the end of the Cold War and the division of Europe. Although approximately 100 people lost their lives attempting to scale the wall, even more people feared that an outright nuclear war would erupt between the superpowers. The peaceful fall of the wall made it clear that positive change was, in fact, possible without the catastrophe of World War Three.

title: The Great Depression
description:
The Great Depression was a massive global economic downturn that began in 1929 and ended about 1939. It is remembered as one of the worst and longest economic depressions of the modern world. Although it began in the US, the economic downturn quickly affected other countries because they were all connected with the US economy through trade and money. This period also experienced massive layoffs of employees, closures of businesses, and reduction of prices to the point where everyone felt the effects of the depression directly.

To begin with, in summer 1929, it was only thought to be another recession and that everything would eventually straighten out on its own. However, from late 1929 through early 1933, everything continued to decline. This meant that factories were not producing as much, banks were failing, and those who lost their jobs had no money to spend, making the economy plummet even further. The U.S. economy gradually began to heal around 1933, only to experience another recession around 1937-1938. Eventually, it was World War II and the huge demand for labor and materials that brought the country out of the Depression.

Each country took turns facing improvements. Britain began to see improvements about 1932 when they abandoned the gold standard. The United States, Canada, and the smaller European nations began to experience improvements in the early 1930s, but these improvements were far from easy. France took much longer to experience improvements, which would not happen until nearly 1938. In one way or another, everybody suffered due to unemployment, poverty, or insecurity, no matter where they lived.

The Great Depression was caused directly as a result of the crash of the stock market in 1929. During the 1920s, the price of stocks escalated, and people bought stocks on margin. This means people bought stocks using money they didn't actually have. People got panicky as the prices began falling. On days like Black Thursday, people ran to unload their stocks before they lost all their wealth. During this period of September through November of 1929, the stock market lost a third of its value. With many nations interdependent upon the economy of the U.S., the chain reaction resulted in the most severe economic crisis of the 20th century.

title: D-Day Invasion of Juno Beach
description:
On June 5, 1944, in the area of Southampton in England, troops of the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division and the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade embarked on boats to prepare for the largest task of the Second World War. This was part of D-Day, the massive invasion of Nazi-occupied France by the Allies. The journey was rough, with large waves that made the voyage difficult for soldiers, and most of them were nervous but understood that their task was of high importance. Much of the information about the invasion was classified, and some of the officers received information when already aboard.

Through the night preceding the landing operations and into the early morning, the Royal Canadian Air Force’s 6 group bombarded German artillery positions located in areas such as Franceville, Merville, and Houlgate with thousands of tons of bombs. At the same time, resistance fighters of France had launched over a thousand acts of sabotage that included blowing up train tracks, cutting communication lines, and any other form of mayhem they could cause at German lines in order to soften their defenses so that those on the beaches had an easier time landing.

Juno Beach was one of five major points of entry along the coast of Normandy. As forces were assaulting Juno Beach, other forces of the British were landing at Sword Beaches as well as Gold Beaches, while American forces were assaulting Omaha Beaches and Utah Beaches. All of it was precisely planned to ensure that these assaults were executed simultaneously, catching the Germans off guard and allowing the Allies to gain a firm ground in France. This was aimed at creating a new front in Europe to squeeze Germany from all sides.

The D-Day operation of Juno Beach is remembered as one of the significant events of World War II. The Canadian forces had to face intensive fire, mines, and other obstacles, but they managed to struggle through and accomplish all their tasks for the day. The Canadians’ success helped the Allied forces begin the liberation of Western Europe from Nazi rule. The heroism and sacrifice of the Canadians in the battle of Juno Beach had an immense contribution to the Allied victory and the defeat of Germany, resulting in the end of World War II.

title: The Manhattan Project
description:
The Manhattan Project was a very secret, wide-ranging research project conducted by the United States throughout World War II from 1942 until 1945 that resulted in the atomic bombs. It obtained its name from the Manhattan Engineer District, where part of this early work took place at New York City's Columbia University. In the year 1939, American scientists and European refugees began to investigate nuclear fission, anxious that a powerful new kind of nuclear weapon may actually be in the process of development in Germany. In the same year, Albert Einstein signed his famous letter addressed to President Roosevelt, proposing that one bomb based on this new principle would result in an unprecedented catastrophe through a gigantic chain reaction.

However, as the war raged on, it became clear that the Germans were also working on some nuclear endeavors. The U.S., UK, and Canada decided to team up, and in 1943, the three countries formally united their efforts. A central place for the project was created and called the Los Alamos Laboratory in the state of New Mexico, led by scientific director Robert Oppenheimer. This is where scientists from different countries worked together on plans for enriching uranium for a bomb that would be able to be dropped from an airplane at the right speed.

On July 16, 1945, they tested the first atomic bomb in the desert near Alamogordo, in the state of New Mexico. This test was called the Trinity Test. In that test, there was a bright light emission, extreme heat, and a shock wave. Then, there was a huge ball of fire that went up into the air, and it was strong enough to melt sand into glass and blow up a test tower. This indicated that the atomic bomb actually works.

A few weeks later, the United States dropped two atomic bombs on Japan. On August 6, 1945, a bomb nicknamed "Little Boy" was dropped on Hiroshima, killing around 70,000 people instantly and roughly 100,000 by the end of the year. Three days later, on August 9, another bomb called "Fat Man" was dropped on Nagasaki after the original target, Kokura, was covered in clouds. About 40,000 people died right away in Nagasaki, and around 70,000 more died by the end of the year. On the same day as the second bombing, the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. Facing all of this, Japan began surrender talks on August 10 and officially surrendered on September 2, 1945, ending World War II.

Manhattan Project is one of the most significant and debated issues in the history of the world. Manhattan Project led to the end of the war, but it also indicated the power possessed by the humans that can destroy an entire city in an instant. Many people felt that these bombs needed to be deferred and feared the implications of such weapons being developed by other nations too. These implications of the Manhattan Project led to the fear of nuclear war, which gave rise to the Cold War. Many nations, including the US and the Soviet Union, worked to develop even more powerful weapons. The whole world has been facing the repercussions of the Manhattan Project ever since.

title: Operation Barbarossa
description:
Barbarossa was the code name used by the Nazi regime when it decided to invade the Soviet Union. This was one of the most ambitious operations in the field of warfare and proved to be one of the biggest mistakes engaged in by Adolf Hitler. To think that an attack on the Soviet Union would take place was surprising in itself since there had been a non-aggression pact signed by the Soviet Union and Germany back in 1939, in which it had been agreed that no invasion by either party would take place. Despite all this, the attack took place because of the distrust between the leader of the Soviet Union and Adolf Hitler of the Nazi regime.

The invasion was originally scheduled for May 1941 but was postponed until the end of June because Germany became occupied with battles in Yugoslavia and Greece. However, when the invasion actually occurred, Germany deployed about 150 divisions, which totaled 3 million soldiers, in addition to tanks and airplanes. They also received assistance from over 30 divisions of soldiers from Finland and Romania. Hitler believed that the Soviet Union was going to fall easily, and at first, everything seemed in his favor because German troops made substantial gains within the Soviet Union.

However, when the Germans pushed forward, things were beginning to add up against them. Their supply routes had to cover enormous distances, and the Soviet Union turned out to be much bigger and harder than they had anticipated. Then, to top it all off, the German army proved unprepared for the harsh Russian climate. Their tanks and cars were no good in the cold, their guns froze, and the men had inadequate winter uniforms. The Soviets just kept sending in reinforcements and fought back with all their might.

Instead of the quick victory that Operation Barbarossa had expected, it turned into a very long and exhausting fight that the Germans could not win. This invasion failure became one of the most significant reversals in the course of World War II. The Soviet Union started pushing them back after holding off the Germans, taking back their land, and eventually pressing on to Germany itself. Operation Barbarossa continued to be remembered as the major example of disaster to be expected in war when overconfidence, poor planning, and underestimating an enemy take place.

title: The Moon Landing
description:
The mission has in the past represented the first occasion in the history of mankind that humans would land on the moon’s surface. The spacecraft was launched on the 16th of July, 1969, at the precise time of 9:32 a.m. The spacecraft had three crew members, which include Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Mike Collins. There has been a massive number of engineers and scientists apart from the other workforce who has contributed to the development of the rockets, computers, and other machinery that has made the whole venture possible. The whole mission has the main objective or motive of ensuring the commitment that was made by the then president, Mr. Kennedy, that a man would land on the moon by the end of the 1960s.

The Apollo 11 spacecraft approached the moon after four days of traveling. Michael Collins remained in the command module, while Armstrong and Aldrin entered the Eagle, referred to as the “Lunar Module.” The area on the moon that the astronauts would land on had to be a flat region, referred to as the “Sea of Tranquility.” On approaching the moon, they realized that they did not have enough fuel left, an experience that led to a crisis situation. Even when they had seconds left, Armstrong changed the path, resulting in a dramatic approach to land on the moon.

Later on, Neil Armstrong descended down the ladder and became the first human to walk on the moon, uttering the words, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." Soon enough, Buzz Aldrin joined him. The couple spent some hours walking, carrying out experiments, and collecting rock and soil samples. In all, they returned with around 47 pounds of material to Earth for scientists. They also placed a plaque that said they came in peace for all mankind and received a phone call from U.S. President Richard Nixon while standing on the moon.

Landing on the moon is regarded as one of the biggest accomplishments in human history. It encouraged people around the world and helped young people around the globe pursue careers in science and engineering fields because they were encouraged to see the pictures of the blue planet they live on from space and realized just how small and delicate it is to realize that space travel to other planets is feasible and helped the United States demonstrate its power during the space race with the Soviet Union during the Cold War because the moon landing, known as Apollo 11, is remembered as the time when the human species extended the boundaries of our potential.
